catalog_quote: Loan words assimilated into Ebira conform to the syllable structure of the language. Ebira has no stressed syllables like English. VV sequences with high tone followed by low tone occur where there is a stressed syllable in the English words that enter the language. Furthermore, an epenthetic vowel is added initially to any English nominal having an initial consonant because all nominals except bound pronoun objects in Ebira start with a vowel. Another epenthetic vowel is added finally to any English word having a closed syllable because Ebira is an open syllable language. [p. 52] ... Tone in Ebira functions at two distinct levels. new_statements.rule_in_words: Ebira is a register-tone language (three level tones H/M/L, plus high-falling and low-rising kinetic tones and downstep; every syllable bears a tone) and, per the author (a native speaker), has no stressed syllables; the only stress-related effect is that the stressed syllable of an English loanword is mapped onto a VV sequence with H followed by L tone (e.g. John > Ijoonu, police > iporiisi).
new_statements.exceptions: None for native words; the remark is made in the loanword section, where English stress is re-encoded as a HL tone sequence on a geminate vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonology (syllable structure and lexical tone); the stress remark is a passing statement in the loanword section rather than a dedicated suprasegmental analysis, and is phrased comparatively ('no stressed syllables like English'). Author describes his own speech (Obehira, Okene area).
new_statements.identity_note: Adive 1984 describes the author's own speech from Obehira in the Okene area, i.e. the main Ebira (Ebira Tao / Okene) dialect that ebir1243 covers; Scholz 1976 ('Igbira') and Ladefoged 1964 ('Igbirra') use older spellings for the same Okene-area variety. Rolle 2022 notes that nearly all Ebira literature concerns this Okene dialect; the Igu/Opanda/Ebira-Nya (Koto) varieties to the north-east are not described here.
